Tool call: go_search_agent
Tool call input: {'knowledge_bases': ['pubmed_papers'], 'search_rounds_budget': 3, 'search_target': 'Find the paper titled or matching “Is the link between metabolic features and TSH levels in polycystic ovary syndrome modulated by the body weight: an euglycaemic-hyperinsulinaemic clamp study?” Determine study design/population, how TSH relates to metabolic features and whether associations differ by body weight/BMI or obesity, with concrete results and PMID if available.'}

The matching paper is **“The link between metabolic features and TSH levels in polycystic ovary syndrome is modulated by the body weight: an euglycaemic-hyperinsulinaemic clamp study” (PMID: 27511825)**.

It was a 2014 case-control study of 154 young women with Rotterdam-criteria PCOS and 88 controls. Assessments included hormonal and lipid assays, OGTT, and a euglycaemic-hyperinsulinaemic clamp. Subclinical hypothyroidism (SCH) was more prevalent in PCOS than controls (14% vs 1%; P<0.01).

In the PCOS group overall, TSH was positively correlated with fasting glucose, but not with other measured hormonal or metabolic parameters. Results differed by weight category: in obese participants, TSH correlated positively with insulin secretion, insulin resistance, DHEAS, and cortisol, and inversely with oestradiol and SHBG. In nonobese participants, only waist-to-hip ratio correlated with TSH. SCH prevalence was similar in the nonobese and obese groups (14% vs 15%), but SCH was associated with higher insulin, DHEAS, cortisol, and Ferriman–Gallwey score only among obese participants. The available abstract does not report correlation coefficients or BMI cut-offs.

**Yes.** In the clamp study of 154 women with PCOS, the relationship between TSH and metabolic/hormonal features differed by body-weight group. Among obese participants, TSH was associated with insulin secretion and resistance, DHEAS, and cortisol, and inversely associated with oestradiol and SHBG. Among nonobese participants, only waist-to-hip ratio was associated with TSH. The authors’ findings therefore support modulation by body weight, although the abstract does not provide correlation coefficients or BMI cut-offs, and the observational results do not establish causation.

**Study:** PMID 27511825, *The link between metabolic features and TSH levels in polycystic ovary syndrome is modulated by the body weight: an euglycaemic-hyperinsulinaemic clamp study.*

FINAL DECISION: YES
